power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned to one of 16 experimental conditions in a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 betweensubjects factorial design, comprising four independent variables: Harm Severity (High vs. Low), Property Value (High vs. Low), Perspective (First-person vs. Third-person), and Victim Gender (Male vs. Female). In the high-harm conditions, the AV's collision with a pedestrian resulted in a severe brain injury, whereas in the low-harm conditions, it resulted only in minor bruising. In the high-value conditions, the collision resulted in the loss of a high-value vehicle (a limited-edition classic car), conditions. Because the present study uses factorial ANOVA (which was also preregistered) as its primary analytical framework, we report here the sample size required for this analysis. A power analysis conducted prior to preregistration also confirmed that the planned sample size of 351 participants was sufficient for the 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 ANOVA. whereas in the low-value conditions, it resulted in the loss of a lower-value vehicle (a new car).

Participants were recruited through Lancers, a major Japanese online crowdsourcing platform. The required sample size was estimated using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7). For a factorial ANOVA across 16 conditions assuming a small-to-medium effect size (f = 0.15, corresponding to η² ≈ .02), α = .05, and power (1 -β) = .80, a minimum sample size of 351 participants was required. To maximize statistical precision and accommodate an anticipated exclusion rate of up to 40% based on pilot testing, we targeted recruiting up to 100 participants per cell (target N = 1,600) 6 . Recruitment was open for two weeks in November 2025, and a total of 1,424 responses were collected. The survey took an average of 7.83 minutes to complete, and each participant received 160 JPY (equivalent to 1,226 JPY per hour) as compensation.

Participants were recruited in the same manner as Study 1 from Lancers. In the light of the aim of this study, we planned the paired comparison between Study 2 and corresponding conditions in Study 1 (four pairs of low-harm × high-value conditions). The required sample size was estimated using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7) for a one-tailed t-test with an expected effect size of d = 0.8, α = .0125, and power (1 -β) = .80. The significance level reflects a Bonferroni adjustment for multiple pairwise comparisons (four pairs), and the expected effect size was based on results from our pilot study. This calculation indicated that 62 participants were needed per pair (31 per cell). Given the 4 total conditions, the minimum required sample size was 124 participants.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Beyond the Trolley Problem: Investigating Moral Preferences for Avoiding Non-Lethal Human Injury over Property Damage in Autonomous Vehicle Accidents
table.research_questions:
H1 (Human Harm Severity × Property Value Interaction):
Support for the AV choosing Path A (Human Harm) will be highest when Human Harm Severity is Low and Property Value is High.
H2 (Gender Effect):
Support for Path A will be higher when the potential victim is male than when it is female (Awad et al., 2018).
H3 (Perspective Effect):
Participants in the 3rd-person (observer) condition will show higher support for Path A than those in the 1st-person (passenger) condition (Bonnefon et al., 2016).
H4 (Liability Effect):
Introducing owner liability in Study 2 will increase support for Path A (Human Harm) compared to the corresponding no-liability condition in Study 1
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.
table.study_design_overview:
Overall Design
Two studies will be conducted.

Study 1: A 2×2×2×2 between-subjects factorial design with no owner liability.

Study 2: A follow-up study introducing owner liability in selected conditions to examine whether financial responsibility shifts participants’ moral preferences.


We also examine how participants’ justice attitudes (Kitahara & Kojima, 2021) relate to their moral judgments.

Study 1: Factorial Design (No Owner Liability)
Design: 2×2×2×2 between-subjects design (16 conditions).

Independent Variables (IVs) and Levels:

Property Value: High (Limited-edition classic car on display) vs. Low (New car on display).
Harm Victim’s Gender: Male vs. Female.
Perspective: 1st-person (participant as passenger) vs. 3rd-person (participant as observer).
Human Harm Severity: Low (minor bruises) vs. High (death).
Justice Attitude: Measured using Kitahara and Kojima’s (2021) scale.

Scenario Context:
Each participant reads a vignette describing an unavoidable AV accident where the vehicle must choose between two paths:
Path A: Colliding with a pedestrian (causing human harm).
Path B: Colliding with non-owned, valuable property.

Example Vignette 1 (High Property × Low Harm):
 “There are currently two options for the autonomous driving system.
Option A: Maintain the current trajectory and attempt to stop using emergency braking. The vehicle will likely collide with the pedestrian at 10 km/h in this case, causing minor injuries such as bruising.
Option B: Decelerate gradually while turning the steering wheel to the left to avoid the pedestrian. The vehicle will then likely crash into a limited-edition classic car (worth 100 million yen) at 50 km/h at the classic car exhibition, resulting in a total loss.”

Example Vignette 2 (Low Property × High Harm)
“There are currently two options for the autonomous driving system.
Option A: Maintain the current trajectory and attempt to stop using emergency braking. The vehicle will likely ultimately strike the pedestrian at 40 km/h, causing fatal injuries.
Option B: Decelerate gradually while steering left to avoid colliding with the pedestrian. However, the vehicle will likely crash into a new car on display (worth 3 million yen) at 50 km/h in this case, resulting in a total loss.”

Legal Assumption:
The AV owner is explicitly stated to hold no legal liability for damages.

Dependent Variable (DV):
Choice preference for the AV’s path, measured on a 6-point Likert scale.
1 = Strongly support Path A (Human Harm/Death)
6 = Strongly support Path B (Property Damage)

Thus, lower scores indicate greater support for human harm; higher scores indicate greater support for property protection.


Study 2: Follow-up with Owner Liability Introduced

Design: Between-subjects comparison targeting the “High Property Value × Low Human Harm” conditions from Study 1.

Independent Variable:
Legal Assumption: Owner bears financial liability for property damage.

Dependent Variable:
Same 6-point Choice Preference scale as in Study 1.

Justice Attitude:
Measured using Kitahara & Kojima’s (2021) scale.
table.randomization: Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the conditions in both Study 1 and Study 2. In both studies, several attention checks and comprehension checks will be presented in randomized order before the main question. Questions for the Justice Attitude scale will also be randomized.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Recruitment Platform:
Japanese online crowdsourcing platforms (e.g., CrowdWorks, Lancers).

Inclusion Criteria:
Japanese speakers residing in Japan, aged 18 or older.

Payment for Participation: 
Participants will be compensated based on the estimated completion time and in accordance with the legal minimum wage in Japan.

Exclusion Criteria
Participants will be excluded if they:
Fail either any of the attention checks or comprehension checks (e.g., key scenario comprehension).

Complete the survey in under 3 minutes.

Duplicate responses from the same person.

Study Timeline:

Data collection is planned to take place between late October and December 2025.
table.manipulated_variables:
Independent Variables (IVs) and Levels:
Property Value: High (Limited-edition classic car on display) vs. Low (New car on display).


Harm Victim’s Gender: Male vs. Female.


Perspective: 1st-person (participant as passenger) vs. 3rd-person (participant as observer).


Human Harm Severity: Low (minor bruises) vs. High (death).
table.measured_variables:
Dependent Variable (DV):
Choice preference for the AV’s path, measured on a 6-point Likert scale.
1 = Strongly support Path A (Human Harm/Death)


6 = Strongly support Path B (Property Damage)


Thus, lower scores indicate greater support for human harm; higher scores indicate greater support for property protection.

Justice Attitude: Measured using Kitahara and Kojima’s (2021) scale.
table.statistical_tests:
Primary Analysis (Study 1)
2×2×2×2 between-subjects ANOVA on Choice Preference (DV).


Planned Welch t-tests for critical pairs (High Property × Low Harm vs. Low Property × High Harm).


Holm–Bonferroni correction will be applied for multiple comparisons.


Testing:
H1: Interaction of Harm Severity × Property Value.


H2: Main effect of Gender.


H3: Main effect of Perspective.


Primary Analysis (Study 2)
Independent-samples t-test comparing mean Choice Preference between Study 2 (Liability) and corresponding Study 1 (No Liability) conditions.


H4 supported if Study 2 mean score is significantly lower, indicating greater support for Path A (Human Harm).
table.data_exclusion_criteria:
Exclusion Criteria
Participants will be excluded if they:
Fail either any of the attention checks or comprehension checks (e.g., key scenario comprehension).


Complete the survey in under 3 minutes.


Duplicate responses from the same person.
table.exploratory_analyses:
Exploratory analyses will examine:
Potential interactions between Justice Attitude and IVs.
The relative prioritization of human harm and property value may vary depending on an individual's moral framework—specifically, whether they hold consequentialist or deontological attitudes. Therefore, the present study will also assess participants’ attitudes toward justice and explore how these attitudes relate to their decision-making patterns.
table.additional_comments: The study protocol has been approved by the Ethics Committee of Hiroshima University, Japan. Participants will provide electronic informed consent before participation and may withdraw at any time without penalty. No personally identifiable data will be collected
table.sample_size:
Study 1 Target Sample Size:
The required sample size was estimated using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7) for a one-tailed t-test with an expected effect size of d = 0.8, α = .0125, and power (1–β) = .80. This yielded a required sample of 62 participants per pair (31 per cell). The significance level reflects Bonferroni adjustment for multiple pairwise comparisons (four pairs), and the estimated effect size is based on results from our pilot study.


With 16 conditions in total, the required sample size is 496 participants.


To account for possible exclusions—estimated at up to 40% based on the pilot study—we plan to recruit as many participants as our budget allows, up to a total of 1,600 participants (100 per cell).


Participants will be randomly assigned to one of the 16 conditions.


Study 2 Target Sample Size:
Four conditions (High Property × Low Harm × Gender × Perspective).


N = 75 per cell × 4 = 300 participants.


Participants will be randomly assigned to one of 4 conditions.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. #### Code Comments
Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).
#### Missing Files
All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.
#### Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., './files') instead of absolute file paths (e.g., 'C://Lakens/project_dir/files') as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.
#### Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid `setwd()` in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author's own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No `setwd()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid `install.packages()` in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an `renv.lock`/`DESCRIPTION` for R, a `requirements.txt` for Python). No `install.packages()` calls were found in any of the code files.
#### Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 1 code file, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).
#### Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 6 distinct packages/libraries: dplyr, readr, rstatix, stringr, tidyr, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).
#### Reproducible Environment

No `renv.lock` file, `sessionInfo()`/`session_info()` record, or `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an `renv.lock` (via the `renv` package), a `sessionInfo()` text dump, or a `groundhog`/`checkpoint` date-pin alongside the code.

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

#### Careless Responding

15 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

**What this does not cover.** Only 13 of 15 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

reproducibility_check.title: Reproducibility Check
reproducibility_check.summary_text:
-  We assessed AND ran 5 R code files for reproducibility (each in an isolated Docker container).
-  5 of 5 scripts ran without error when executed.
-  6 installable dependencies detected.
- 2392 statistics stored from the extracted output; 35 of 75 reported tests matched (46.7%).

summary_table.ethics_statements: The research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Hiroshima University (HR-PSY-008230).
live_data_statements: The results indicate that participants are more likely to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected harm to humans is relatively low compared to the value of the property.
Participants provided informed consent and were free to withdraw at any time.
Participants were recruited through Lancers, a major Japanese online crowdsourcing platform.
Before applying exclusion criteria based on attention and comprehension checks, we removed participants who completed the survey in under 3 minutes or did not finish the survey.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of 16 experimental conditions in a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 betweensubjects factorial design, comprising four independent variables: Harm Severity (High vs.
In each condition, participants were asked to imagine a situation in which an AV faces a dilemma.

Following this description, participants were presented with a condition-specific image and corresponding alternatives: • Path A: Maintain its trajectory and strike a pedestrian, resulting in [minor bruising / traumatic brain injury].
In total, 20 participants were excluded based on this criterion.
As a result, 674 participants were classified as passers, and the remaining 643 participants were excluded from the main analysis.

There was also a significant main effect of Property Value, F(1, 658) = 11.45, p < .001, η² = .014, such that participants were more likely to endorse harming a pedestrian when the alternative involved damaging a high-value car rather than a low-value one.
Participants were recruited in the same manner as Study 1 from Lancers.
This calculation indicated that 62 participants were needed per pair (31 per cell).
Participants were randomly assigned to one of four conditions:

H2 (Gender Effect) received partial support; while participants were significantly more willing to allow minor harm to male pedestrians than female pedestrians, this effect was weak and predominantly driven by male participants.

In Study 2, when participants were explicitly informed that the AV's passenger would bear legal responsibility for property damage caused by the vehicle, approximately 70% of participants in three of the four conditions preferred allowing the AV to strike a pedestrian to avoid damaging the classic car.

Following the main question, participants completed two comprehension tasks regarding the scenario: C1: If the autonomous vehicle continues straight without braking, the pedestrian will be killed.C2: By applying sudden braking, the autonomous vehicle can avoid colliding with the pedestrian.Participants indicated their agreement on a 6-point scale (1 = Strongly disagree to6 = Strongly agree).

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 5 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:5, File = c("Screening_Study1.R", "Study1_Table.R", 
"Screening_Study2.R", "Table_Study2.R", "Paired_Comparison_Ttest.R"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "Screening_Study1.R", "—", "Screening_Study2.R", 
"Screening_Study1.R, Screening_Study2.R"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"dependency", "numeric", "dependency", "dependency")), row.names = c(NA, 
-5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 5 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Screening_Study1.R", "Study1_Table.R", 
"Screening_Study2.R", "Table_Study2.R", "Paired_Comparison_Ttest.R"
), Outcome = c("ran_ok", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "ran_ok"
), Detail = c("", "", "", "", ""), "Time (s)" = c(1.5, 1.4, 1.4, 
1.4, 2.4)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```

text.text: Given the rapid development of autonomous vehicle (AV) technologies, recent studies, such as the Moral Machine Experiment, have examined people's moral judgments in trolley-style dilemmas, where AVs must choose between unavoidable outcomes, often involving whether to change course to save a greater number of lives.
However, fatal injuries represent only a subset of harms caused by traffic agents; most traffic accidents are non-fatal or involve only property damage.

The present study focuses on trade-offs between human harm and property damage, examining whether the principle of the priority of human over property (PPHP)-reflected in some ethical and legal guidelines-is consistently supported by laypeople.
Across a series of online experiments, we investigated whether people's path preferences in scenarios where an AV must choose between avoiding human harm and avoiding property damage align with PPHP.

We manipulated several factors, including the severity of harm to the pedestrian, the value of the property, the observer's perspective (first-person vs. thirdperson), the gender of the potential victim, and whether the passenger would bear legal liability.
The results indicate that participants are more likely to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected harm to humans is relatively low compared to the value of the property.
This tendency is amplified when passengers are held legally liable and among participants with more utilitarian moral attitudes.
These findings suggest that AV behavior strictly guided by PPHP is not always supported by folk moral preferences.

As autonomous vehicles (AVs) become more integrated into society, the question of how they should behave in unavoidable accident scenarios has become central to ethical debates and policy-making surrounding them.

A large portion of existing research has focused on extreme moral dilemmas involving life-and-death trade-offs, often drawing on variations of the classic "trolley problem" (Awad et al., 2018; Bonnefon et al., 2016).
text.formatted: A large portion of existing research has focused on extreme moral dilemmas involving life-and-death trade-offs, often drawing on variations of the classic "trolley problem" <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Awad et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bonnefon et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: 1 While these studies have generated valuable insights, fatal accidents are just a part of the total number of traffic accidents.

According to WHO (World Health Organization, 2023), approximately 1.19 million people die as a result of road traffic crashes each year, while an additional 20-50 million people suffer non-fatal injuries.
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr">WHO (World Health Organization, 2023)</ref>, approximately 1.19 million people die as a result of road traffic crashes each year, while an additional 20-50 million people suffer non-fatal injuries.

text.text: Real-world AV accidents are likewise unlikely to be limited to fatal outcomes; they are expected to more frequently involve non-fatal forms of harm, such as minor or serious injuries, as well as substantial property damage.
The increasing deployment of AVs may therefore give rise to moral dilemmas that extend beyond life-and-death scenarios, such as choosing between killing one person and killing five.
AVs may also face, and perhaps more frequently, non-fatal moral dilemmas involving trade-offs between human harm and property damage.
Several plausible scenarios illustrate how such dilemmas could arise in the near future.
For example, when an autonomous bus performs an emergency stop to avoid colliding with an external object, standing passengers inside the vehicle may fall and suffer serious injuries.
Avoiding damage to the external object may come at the cost of causing non-fatal harm to passengers.

Similarly, the emergence of small-scale autonomous vehicles, such as autonomous delivery robots and autonomous personal mobility devices (e.g., autonomous electric wheelchairs), makes trade-offs between human harm and property damage increasingly plausible.

Because such vehicles are generally smaller and slower than conventional automobiles, they are less likely to cause fatal injuries to pedestrians but may more frequently encounter situations in which minor human harm must be weighed against property damage.

1 Some argue that such trolley-style dilemmas are unrealistic; for example, Cecchini et al. (2025) argue that most trolley-style dilemmas, including those used in the Moral Machine Experiment, are far removed from real-world traffic situations.
text.formatted: 1 Some argue that such trolley-style dilemmas are unrealistic; for example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cecchini et al. (2025)</ref> argue that most trolley-style dilemmas, including those used in the Moral Machine Experiment, are far removed from real-world traffic situations.

text.text: However, they are increasingly recognized as practical concerns, as reflected in existing legal frameworks.

For instance, German regulations on autonomous driving explicitly address such dilemmas, indicating that these conflict scenarios are considered realistic and in need of normative guidance (AFGBV, Annex 1, Part 1, No.

Despite the importance of such trade-offs, prior research has largely focused on folk moral judgments concerning fatal AV dilemmas, with relatively little attention paid to non-fatal accident scenarios.
Against this backdrop, the present study investigates folk moral judgments about non-fatal accidents involving AVs, 2 with a particular focus on trade-offs between human harm and property damage.
More specifically, we examine three questions.

First, we investigate whether people consistently prioritize avoiding harm to humans over avoiding property damage, and whether this priority is robust to variations in the value of the property and the severity of the potential human harm.

Second, we examine whether these judgments are influenced by contextual factors, including legal liability, the perspective from which participants evaluate the scenario (first-person vs. third-person), and the gender of the potential victim (male vs. female).
Third, we investigate whether individual differences in justice attitudes are associated with preferences concerning how an AV should behave in such situations.
We conducted two studies.

Study 1 employed a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects design to examine how harm severity, property value, victim gender, and perspective affect moral preferences (i.e., path preferences) in AV accident scenarios in which the vehicle owner bears no legal liability.
Study 2 introduced owner liability in selected conditions to investigate whether legal responsibility shifts people's moral preferences.

Together, the two studies suggest that people's moral preferences are sensitive to the relative severity of human harm and property damage: participants tended to prioritize avoiding property damage when the expected human harm was minor and the property damage was substantial.
Furthermore, participants' justice attitudes, specifically the extent to which they endorsed deontological or utilitarian principles, were associated with their moral preferences.
The main aim of this study is to investigate folk moral path preferences about trade-offs between nonfatal human harm and property damage.

Specifically, this study examines whether the following principle is consistently supported across different situations, and to what extent it is robustly For the purpose of this study, we take PPHP as a guiding principle for all traffic agents, including AVs.

According to PPHP, when an AV faces an either-or situation-namely, whether to collide with a human or with property-it should always choose to avoid human harm and instead damage the property, regardless of the severity of the expected human harm or the value of the property involved.

Indeed, some ethical guidelines for AVs explicitly state that human life or safety should be prioritized over property in unavoidable accidents (e.g., Ethics Commission of the BMVI, 2017; International Organization for Standardization, 2023).
A similar principle is reflected in German law.
Section 1e(2)2(b) of the German Road Traffic Act (Straßenverkehrsgesetz) stipulates that when conflicting legal interests are unavoidably at stake, human life takes precedence.
However, it remains unclear whether, and to what extent, laypeople's moral preferences support such a principle.

We do not assume that public moral preferences play a decisive role in normative debate, but if a substantial proportion of people do not consistently endorse PPHP, this would provide at least a prima facie reason to reconsider whether PPHP is an appropriate principle for guiding the behaviour of AVs (we will discuss this point more in detail in section 5).
Against this backdrop, the present study examines people's path preferences in dilemma situations in which they must choose between harming a human and damaging property.

We conducted two studies to examine whether people's path preferences in these situations are influenced by human harm severity (high/low), property value (high/low), judgment perspectives (first/third) and legal liability (liable/not liable), and victim gender (male/female).

If PPHP is robustly endorsed and laypeople's path preferences are stable, people should consistently prioritize the avoidance of human harm over property damage, regardless of variations in the severity of human harm and the value of the property.

However, if moral judgments reflect a systematic evaluation of overall outcomes and trade-offs, preferences should vary substantially depending on the magnitude of physical harm relative to material loss; both decreased human harm severity and increased property value are expected to, combined together, lead to increased support for an AV choosing to avoid property damage.

In our 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 research design, it is predicted as followsfoot_0 : • H1: Support for an AV choosing to avoid property damage will be highest when human harm severity is low and property value is high.
text.formatted: In our 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 research design, it is predicted as follows<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> : • H1: Support for an AV choosing to avoid property damage will be highest when human harm severity is low and property value is high.

text.text: More precisely, H1 is supported by the following main-effect predictions regarding people's path preferences: • H1a: Support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path will be higher when human harm severity is low (minor injury) than when it is high (severe/fatal injury).
• H1b: Support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path will be higher when property value is high than when it is low.
Additionally, path preferences may be influenced by the demographic characteristics of potential victims, the decision-making perspective, and the legal allocation of financial burdens.

In line with previous literature on moral trade-offs (Awad et al., 2018; Bonnefon et al., 2016), we hypothesized: • H2: Support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path will be higher when the potential victim is male than when the potential victim is female.
text.formatted: In line with previous literature on moral trade-offs <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Awad et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bonnefon et al., 2016)</ref>, we hypothesized: • H2: Support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path will be higher when the potential victim is male than when the potential victim is female.

text.text: • H3: Participants in the third-person (observer) condition will show higher support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path than those in the first-person (passenger) condition.
• H4: Introducing owner liability will increase support for avoiding property damage and choosing the human-harm path compared to the corresponding no-liability condition.
To test these hypotheses, we conducted two experiments.
In both studies, we investigated people's path preferences in dilemma scenarios in which an AV must choose between harming a human and damaging property.

The original hypotheses (H1, H2, H3 and H4) 4 and analysis plans were preregistered on OSF. 5 Two main-effect hypotheses regarding harm severity (H1a) and property value (H1b) were added to evaluate the Priority of Human over Property (PPHP) principle more directly in the drafting process.
text.formatted: The original hypotheses (H1, H2, H3 and H4) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">4</ref> and analysis plans were preregistered on OSF. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_2">5</ref> Two main-effect hypotheses regarding harm severity (H1a) and property value (H1b) were added to evaluate the Priority of Human over Property (PPHP) principle more directly in the drafting process.

text.text: In Study 1, we manipulated four variables-human harm severity, property value, victim gender, and decision-making perspective-to test H1, H2, and H3, yielding a total of 16 conditions.
In Study 2, to test H4, we manipulated liability conditions in the scenarios.
While the scenarios in Study 1 explicitly stated that passengers bore no liability for the harm caused by the vehicle, those in Study 2 explicitly stated that passengers were liable for such harm.
We focused on the low human harm × high property value condition and conducted pairwise comparisons between Study 2 and the corresponding condition in Study 1.
In addition to these factors, people's broader normative beliefs may also shape their decisions.

To investigate the relationship between individuals' normative commitments and their moral judgments involving non-fatal harm caused by AVs, we included the Japanese version of the Justice Attitudes Scale developed by Kitaori and Kojima (2021) in both Study 1 and Study 2.
text.formatted: To investigate the relationship between individuals' normative commitments and their moral judgments involving non-fatal harm caused by AVs, we included the Japanese version of the Justice Attitudes Scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Kitaori and Kojima (2021)</ref> in both Study 1 and Study 2.

text.text: For the justice-attitude variables, we preregistered exploratory analyses but did not preregister specific hypotheses.
The research protocol was approved by the Ethics Committee of Hiroshima University (HR-PSY-008230).
Participants provided informed consent and were free to withdraw at any time.
>Experiments  >Study 1  >Materials and Methods
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Experiments</head> <head n="3.1." >Study 1</head> <head n="3.1.1." >Materials and Methods</head>

text.text: Participants were recruited through Lancers, a major Japanese online crowdsourcing platform.
The required sample size was estimated using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7).

For a factorial ANOVA across 16 conditions assuming a small-to-medium effect size (f = 0.15, corresponding to η² ≈ .02), α = .05, and power (1 -β) = .80, a minimum sample size of 351 participants was required.
To maximize statistical precision and accommodate an anticipated exclusion rate of up to 40% based on pilot testing, we targeted recruiting up to 100 participants per cell (target N = 1,600) 6 .
text.formatted: To maximize statistical precision and accommodate an anticipated exclusion rate of up to 40% based on pilot testing, we targeted recruiting up to 100 participants per cell (target N = 1,600) <ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">6</ref> .

text.text: Recruitment was open for two weeks in November 2025, and a total of 1,424 responses were collected.
The survey took an average of 7.83 minutes to complete, and each participant received 160 JPY (equivalent to 1,226 JPY per hour) as compensation.
Before applying exclusion criteria based on attention and comprehension checks, we removed participants who completed the survey in under 3 minutes or did not finish the survey.
This resulted in a final sample of 1,337 participants (Male = 741, Female = 591, Other/No Answer = 5; M age = 44.40, SD = 10.87).
Study 1 employed a 2×2×2×2 between-subjects factorial design with the following factors: • Property Value: High vs.
Low • Harm Severity: Low vs.
High • Victim Gender: Male vs.
Female • Perspective: First-person (passenger) vs.
Third-person (observer) All scenarios explicitly stated that the AV owner had no legal liability for any resulting property damage.
Participants were randomly assigned to one of 16 experimental conditions in a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 betweensubjects factorial design, comprising four independent variables: Harm Severity (High vs.
Low), Property Value (High vs.
Low), Perspective (First-person vs.
Third-person), and Victim Gender (Male vs.

Across conditions, participants' preferences varied systematically with Harm Severity.

When harm to the pedestrian was described as severe, the mean score was relatively high (M = 5.16, SD = 1.05), indicating greater support for the property-damage path, whereas substantially lower mean ratings were observed when the harm was non-fatal (M = 3.98, SD = 1.51), indicating greater support for the human-harm path.

We conducted a 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 between-subjects ANOVA with Harm Severity, Property Value, Victim Gender, and Perspective as factors.
The analysis was conducted using JASP (version 0.95.4).
The analysis revealed several significant main effects but no significant interactions.

There was a strong main effect of Harm Severity, F(1, 658) = 143.90, p < .001, η² = .173, indicating that participants showed substantially greater support for the human-harm path when the harm described was non-fatal rather than fatal.

text.text: The main effect of Gender was also significant, F(1, 658) = 8.84, p = .003, η² = .011; participants showed greater support for harming a male pedestrian than a female pedestrian, consistent with H2.

Interestingly, the main effect of Victim Gender appeared to be driven primarily by judgments made by male participants.

To examine this more closely, we re-ran the ANOVA after excluding five participants who selected "Other/No Answer" for their own gender and included participants' gender as an additional independent variable (this analysis was not preregistered).
Although the main effect of Victim Gender remained statistically significant, its magnitude was considerably reduced, F(1, 639) = 7.200, p = .007, η² = .009.

H1a and H1b have been confirmed: Descriptive statistics and ANOVA suggest that people's pathpreference ratings are influenced by both Harm Severity and Property Value.
Lower harm severity and high property value are associated with increased support for the human-harm path.

Descriptive statistics also support H1: support for the human-harm path was consistently higher in Low-Harm × High-Value conditions than in other conditions, which can be explained as the combined effects of H1a and H1b.
In contrast, H2 has only been partially validated, and H3 has not been supported.

While we found that participants tend to prefer the property-damage path and prioritize the avoidance of human harm when the victim's gender was female, this effect was primarily driven by male participants only.
Moreover, our analysis using ANOVA suggests that people's path preferences are not significantly influenced by their judgment perspectives, which does not align with H3.
In Study 1, all scenarios explicitly stated that passengers would bear no liability for any harm caused by the AV in the event of an accident.
Even under these conditions, quite a number of participants supported the human-harm path in the Low-Harm × High-Value conditions.
However, approximately 47-65% of participants still endorsed the property-damage path.
As hypothesized (H4), if individuals are assigned liability for harm caused by AVs, their priority preferences may shift.

Accordingly, Study 2 examined whether assigning liability to passengers for harm caused by AVs influences moral preferences regarding the vehicle's course of actionspecifically, whether participants show a clearer tendency to prefer the human-harm path when passengers bear liability.

text.text: Participants were recruited in the same manner as Study 1 from Lancers.
In the light of the aim of this study, we planned the paired comparison between Study 2 and corresponding conditions in Study 1 (four pairs of low-harm × high-value conditions).
The required sample size was estimated using G*Power (version 3.1.9.7) for a one-tailed t-test with an expected effect size of d = 0.8, α = .0125, and power (1 -β) = .80.
The significance level reflects a Bonferroni adjustment for multiple pairwise comparisons (four pairs), and the expected effect size was based on results from our pilot study.
This calculation indicated that 62 participants were needed per pair (31 per cell).
Given the 4 total conditions, the minimum required sample size was 124 participants.
To account for potential exclusions-estimated at up to 50% based on Study 1-we planned to recruit as many as 400 participants.
Recruitment was open for one day in December 2025, and a total of 400 responses were collected.
The survey took an average of 7.45 minutes to complete, and each participant received 160 JPY (equivalent to 1,288 JPY per hour) as compensation.
Before applying exclusion criteria based on attention and comprehension checks, we removed participants who completed the survey in under 3 minutes or did not finish the survey.
This resulted in a final sample of 375 participants (Male = 236, Female = 138, Other/No Answer = 1; M age = 44.12, SD = 10.33).

Overall, our experiments provided varying degrees of support for our predictions, with some differences between the preregistered hypotheses.

H1 (including H1a and H1b) was fully supported: support for choosing the human-harm path to avoid property damage was descriptively highest in the Low Harm × High Value conditions, and significant main effects of both Harm Severity and Property
Value were observed, consistent with H1a and H1b.

H2 (Gender Effect) received partial support; while participants were significantly more willing to allow minor harm to male pedestrians than female pedestrians, this effect was weak and predominantly driven by male participants.
In contrast, H3 (Perspective Effect) was not supported, as path preferences did not significantly differ between the first-person passenger and third-person observer perspectives.

Finally, H4 (Liability Effect) was partially supported: introducing passenger liability systematically shifted preferences toward prioritizing property over human harm, with the increase reaching statistical significance in two of the four target conditions after Bonferroni correction.
To reiterate, the primary aim of this study was to investigate the consistency between folk moral preferences and PPHP in non-fatal, unavoidable AV accident scenarios.

Specifically, we examined whether people consistently prioritize the avoidance of human harm over the avoidance of property damage across different levels of property value and human injury severity, as well as across different perspectives, victim genders, and liability conditions.
The overall support for H1, H1a, and H1b, together with partial support for H2 and H4, provides at least two insights into our original research question.
First and foremost, the overall support for H1 strongly suggests that PPHP is not unconditionally supported by folk moral preferences.

In Study 1, when the potential victim was male, more than 50% of participants preferred avoiding damage to the vehicle in the Low Harm × High Value condition, allowing the AV to strike the pedestrian.

These results suggest that people do not necessarily expect AVs to prioritize the avoidance of human harm at all costs when faced with a dilemma involving potential harm to a human and damage to valuable property.
Second, the partial support for H4 suggests that people's support for PPHP depends on the financial burden associated with AV-caused damage.

In Study 2, when participants were explicitly informed that the AV's passenger would bear legal responsibility for property damage caused by the vehicle, approximately 70% of participants in three of the four conditions preferred allowing the AV to strike a pedestrian to avoid damaging the classic car.

These results suggest that public support for PPHP in unavoidable AV accidents depends, at least in part, on the extent to which individuals themselves bear legal and financial responsibility for damage caused by AVs.
These psychological findings have several ethical implications.

First, assuming that folk moral judgments play an evidential role in ethical theorizing, our study casts doubt on the validity of PPHP, as it suggests that folk path preferences depart from PPHP in some cases. 7 Moreover, given that people's path preferences are influenced by liability conditions, PPHP may be socially acceptable only if appropriate institutional mechanisms are in place to compensate for damage caused by AVs.
text.formatted: First, assuming that folk moral judgments play an evidential role in ethical theorizing, our study casts doubt on the validity of PPHP, as it suggests that folk path preferences depart from PPHP in some cases. <ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">7</ref> Moreover, given that people's path preferences are influenced by liability conditions, PPHP may be socially acceptable only if appropriate institutional mechanisms are in place to compensate for damage caused by AVs.

text.text: That said, the fact that PPHP is not consistently supported by a majority of people does not immediately imply that PPHP is unjustified or should be abandoned.
This is because folk moral preferences in individual cases constitute only one consideration in ethical theorizing (cf. Savulescu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is because folk moral preferences in individual cases constitute only one consideration in ethical theorizing (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Savulescu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: While such preferences may serve as inputs into moral deliberation, ethical principles are developed in light of moral preferences across different contexts and multiple normative considerations.

For instance, although our results suggest that people prioritize the avoidance of property damage over the avoidance of human harm in some individual cases, they do not establish that people reject PPHP as a general principle.
Even if people prioritize property over human harm in particular cases, their preferences may differ when they are asked to endorse a rule for implementation across society as a whole.
If a majority of people endorse prioritizing the avoidance of human harm as a general rule for society, this commitment may outweigh their preferences in individual cases.
Indeed, some morally discriminatory preferences in the context of AVs are likely to be rejected in light of more general moral commitments.
Current ethical debates surrounding AV regulation already regard certain distinctions as morally unacceptable.
Ethical guidelines, such as Ethics of Connected and Automated Vehicles (European Commission, 2020), explicitly prohibit the consideration of gender in crash-avoidance programming.
By contrast, our results suggest that male participants tend to prioritize female pedestrians over male pedestrians, a finding consistent with those reported in MME.

Although these empirical findings provide support for a female-prioritizing norm, their evidential weight as inputs into moral deliberation may be undermined by people's commitment to equality or impartiality in mobility contexts, as suggested by several studies (Bigman & Gray, 2020; Paulo et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Although these empirical findings provide support for a female-prioritizing norm, their evidential weight as inputs into moral deliberation may be undermined by people's commitment to equality or impartiality in mobility contexts, as suggested by several studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bigman & Gray, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Paulo et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, the evidential weight of the path preferences conflicting with PPHP identified in our study might also be undermined by more fundamental moral commitments that support PPHP.
The influence of morally irrelevant factors may also undermine the evidential significance of folk moral judgments.

MME found that people's path preferences are influenced by factors such as gender, social status, and physical characteristics (Awad et al., 2018). Cecchini et al. (2025) argue that such results are "probably discriminative and activate implicit biases in participants" (p. 1040).

(2025)</ref> argue that such results are "probably discriminative and activate implicit biases in participants" (p. 1040).

text.text: Although our results indicate that people's path preferences are relatively robust to certain framing variations, such as differences in perspective, they may nevertheless be explained, at least in part, by the influence of biasing factors.
In summary, although our study demonstrates that PPHP does not fully align with folk moral preferences, further theoretical and empirical investigation is needed before drawing normative conclusions.

Theoretically, we need to evaluate whether people's path preferences that prioritize property value provide sufficient reason to abandon PPHP, particularly in light of other moral principles and the expected consequences of implementing alternative principles.
Empirically, we need to investigate the evidential weight of these preferences.

This includes further investigations of path preferences in non-lethal scenarios, relevant moral commitments (e.g., whether people support the implementation of ethical norms that conflict with PPHP), and the robustness of these preferences (e.g., their susceptibility to biases and other distorting factors).

That said, at the very least, our experimental results suggest that if PPHP is to remain a foundational principle of AV regulation, its proponents may be required to provide reasons for dismissing folk moral preferences that prioritize the avoidance of property damage.
This, in turn, motivates further research into folk moral preferences in non-lethal AV accidents.
Before concluding, several limitations should be noted.
First, our sample was limited to Japanese participants.
The generalizability of our findings requires cross-cultural investigation.
Similarly, as noted at the beginning of this section, our experiments focused on a limited range of scenarios.
It remains unclear to what extent support for (or opposition to) PPHP generalizes across different types of non-fatal, unavoidable traffic accidents involving AVs.
More comprehensive studies that include a wider variety of non-fatal accident scenarios are necessary.
Second, our experiments employed vignette-based surveys that required participants to understand relatively complex hypothetical scenarios.
The overall comprehension rate was relatively low.
This raises the possibility that some participants may have passed the comprehension checks without fully understanding the scenarios, potentially threatening the reliability of our findings.
In this respect, it may be helpful in future studies to use video materials instead of text-based vignettes, or to combine video and textual presentations.

Some recent studies in experimental moral philosophy have indeed employed video materials to improve participants' comprehension of vignette scenarios (e.g., Inarimori et al., 2024; Lim et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Some recent studies in experimental moral philosophy have indeed employed video materials to improve participants' comprehension of vignette scenarios (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Inarimori et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Lim et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Third, it is important to acknowledge an inherent methodological limitation of our experimental design.

Our study is essentially an application of the so-called "trolley problem," originally introduced by Foot (1967) and later developed by Thomson (1985), in which individuals are asked whether they would violate a moral norm in order to maximize overall utility.
text.formatted: Our study is essentially an application of the so-called "trolley problem," originally introduced by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Foot (1967)</ref> and later developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Thomson (1985)</ref>, in which individuals are asked whether they would violate a moral norm in order to maximize overall utility.

text.text: However, some scholars have criticized the use of this paradigm to investigate people's moral judgments about AVs.

For example, Cecchini et al. (2025) argue that studies employing trolley-type scenarios, such as the Moral Machine Experiment (Awad et al., 2018), fail to adequately capture people's moral judgments about AV accidents due to their lack of realism.
text.formatted: For example, <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cecchini et al. (2025)</ref> argue that studies employing trolley-type scenarios, such as the Moral Machine Experiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Awad et al., 2018)</ref>, fail to adequately capture people's moral judgments about AV accidents due to their lack of realism.

text.text: Most trolley dilemma cases, including those used in the Moral Machine Experiment, are far removed from real-world traffic situations.
Although analogous situations may arise, real-world traffic accidents typically involve a wider range of possible actions and constraints than those presented in stylized dilemma scenarios.
According to Cecchini et al. (2025), this lack of realism makes it difficult to measure people's considered moral judgments (see also Bauman et al., 2014).
text.formatted: According to <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Cecchini et al. (2025)</ref>, this lack of realism makes it difficult to measure people's considered moral judgments (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Bauman et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: To address this concern, several recent studies on folk moral judgments involving AVs have employed VR technology (Li et al., 2019; Meder et al., 2019; Sütfeld et al., 2017).
text.formatted: To address this concern, several recent studies on folk moral judgments involving AVs have employed VR technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Li et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Meder et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Sütfeld et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Furthermore, some recent studies have shifted their focus to participants' risk preferences in potential collisions with other road users, rather than directly asking path preferences under deterministic situations (Krügel & Uhl, 2024).
text.formatted: Furthermore, some recent studies have shifted their focus to participants' risk preferences in potential collisions with other road users, rather than directly asking path preferences under deterministic situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Krügel & Uhl, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: We do not deny that these concerns may limit the evidential value of responses obtained from trolley-style vignettes.

However, as noted at the outset of this paper, trolley-like dilemmas are increasingly recognized as practically relevant, and there are realistic scenarios in which AVs may face trade-offs between property damage and human harm.
Moreover, this study used a vignette-based design to examine folk moral preferences in specific contexts.
Text-based vignettes are an effective means of manipulating the details of the situations presented to participants, thereby enabling precise control of the independent variables.

At the same time, we sought to enhance the realism of our scenarios as much as possible-for example, by explicitly specifying that hard braking was incompatible with changing direction and combining pictures with text vignettes.

Although we acknowledge that our design does not entirely address concerns about ecological validity, we believe that these concerns do not seriously undermine the importance of our experimental findings regarding folk moral preferences in non-fatal situations.
We investigated folk moral path preferences in non-fatal accident scenarios among Japanese participants.
Our results show that people prioritize avoiding property damage rather than human harm depending on the expected severity of human injury and the value of the property at stake.
We also found that such preferences are more pronounced when passengers are held liable.
Although our studies focus exclusively on specific scenarios and a single demographic group, our findings provide a prima facie reason to reconsider the validity of PPHP.

If people are willing to endorse choices that violate PPHP in certain situations, its proponents should explain why PPHP should nevertheless be adopted despite its apparent divergence from folk moral preferences.
Addressing this question requires further theoretical reflection on the compatibility of such preferences with other normative principles, as well as further empirical investigation.

Future studies should examine the robustness of folk moral path preferences across a wider range of non-fatal scenarios, their relative strength compared with other moral commitments, the extent to which they translate into support for general ethical principles, and their susceptibility to morally irrelevant considerations.

text.text: Similar to Study 1, the following analyses are based on participants who passed all comprehension and attention checks (N = 211).

All analyses were conducted using R (version 4.5.1) Across all conditions, mean support for the human-harm path was notably higher (indicated by lower mean ratings) compared to the corresponding conditions in Study 1, where no liability was assigned.
The mean ratings for the four conditions ranged from 2.96 to 3.29 on a 6-point scale.
When the potential victim was male, mean support for the human-harm path was almost identical across both the first-person perspective and the third-person perspective.
In these conditions, approximately 69% of participants indicated support for the human-harm path over the property damage path.

When the potential victim was female, participants in the third-person perspective showed a stronger preference for the human-harm path (68.3% support for the human-harm path) than those in the firstperson perspective (48.8% support for the human-harm path).

Notably, the First-Person/Female condition was the only group where the majority of participants still favored the property damage path (51.2%), although the proportion was considerably smaller than in Study 1.

The primary focus of this paper is on Level 4 and Level 5 systems, which do not require human drivers to take control or intervene. supported or influenced by contextual factors: Principle of Priority of Human over Property (PPHP): Human harm should always take precedence over property damage.

Following the main question, participants completed two comprehension tasks regarding the scenario: C1: If the autonomous vehicle continues straight without braking, the pedestrian will be killed.C2: By applying sudden braking, the autonomous vehicle can avoid colliding with the pedestrian.Participants indicated their agreement on a 6-point scale (1 = Strongly disagree to6 = Strongly agree).

For ease of interpretation, we use the terms "Human-Harm Path" and "Property-Damage Path" in what follows, instead of "Path A" and "Path B." Also, we refer to the main dependent variable (participants' ratings on the 6-point Likert scale measuring path preference) as "Path Preference Ratings."

In this study, the left end of the path preference Likert scale (1) corresponds to "strong support for the human-harm path," and the right end (6) corresponds to "strong support for the property-damage path."

Accordingly, mean ratings between 1 and 3 indicate overall support for the Human-Harm Path (Path A), whereas mean ratings between 4 and 6 indicate overall support for the Property-Damage Path (Path B).

In other words, higher ratings indicate greater support for the avoidance of human harm (the property-damage path), whereas lower ratings indicate greater support for the avoidance of property damage (the human-harm path).
